---
<!-- question-1: body_md -->
\label{main-question}
Is $\mathcal{K}({X})$ plastic whenever $X$ is plastic?
<!-- end question-1 -->
<!-- question-2: body_md -->
\label{graph-question}
Let $G$ be a plastic connected graph, endowed with the unweighted path
metric. Is $\mathcal{K}({G})$ plastic?
<!-- end question-2 -->
<!-- theorem--1: body_md -->
Let $G$ be a connected, locally finite, regular graph. Then $\mathcal{K}({G})$ is
plastic.
<!-- end theorem--1 -->
<!-- theorem--2: body_md -->
Let $(K,d_K)$ be a compact connected metric space and let $(L,d_L)$ satisfy
the following conditions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $d_L(u,v)\ge1$ for all distinct $u,v\in L$, and every bounded subset
of $L$ is finite.
\item For every nonexpansive bijection $h$ of $\mathcal{K}({L})$, there exist a
bijective isometry $g\colon L\to L$ and nonempty finite sets
$L_1\subseteq L_2\subseteq\cdots$, with $\bigcup_nL_n=L$, such that
\[
h[\mathcal{K}({L_n})]=\mathcal{K}({g[L_n]})\qquad(n\ge1).
\]
\end{enumerate}
Then $\mathcal{K}({K\times L})$ is plastic.
<!-- end theorem--2 -->
<!-- corollary--1: body_md -->
Let $K$ be a compact connected metric space and let $G$ be an infinite
connected, locally finite, regular graph. Then $\mathcal{K}({K\times G})$ is plastic.
In particular, $\mathcal{K}({K\times T_k})$ is plastic for every regular tree $T_k$ of
degree $k\ge2$.
<!-- end corollary--1 -->
<!-- theorem--3: body_md -->
Let $G$ be an infinite connected, locally finite graph, $k$ its minimum
degree and $G'=\{v:\deg(v)=k\}$. If $G'$ is finite, then both $G$ and
$\mathcal{K}({G})$ are plastic.
<!-- end theorem--3 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{general_fact_injectivity}
Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and let $f\colon X\to X$ be a nonexpansive injection.
Then for every $x\in X$ and $r>0$, we have $f[\overline{B}({x, r})]\subset\overline{B}({f(x), r})$. In particular, $|\overline{B}({x, r})|\le|\overline{B}({f(x), r})|$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
See \cite[Lemma 3.1]{hida2026plasticity}.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{tb-plastic}
Every totally bounded metric space is plastic. In particular, every finite metric
space is plastic.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{hyper-total-bound}
Let $X$ be a totally bounded metric space. Then $\mathcal{K}({X})$ is plastic.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
See \cite[Proposition 2.5]{hida2026plasticity}.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:hyperball}
Let $X$ be a metric space, let $\mathcal{K}({X})$ be its hyperspace, and let $A\in\mathcal{K}({X})$ and $n>0$. Then
for $U\in\mathcal{K}({X})$,
\[
d_H(A,U)\le n
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
U\subseteq\bigcup_{a\in A}\overline{B}({a, n})
\ \ \text{ and }\ \
U\cap\overline{B}({a, n})\ne\emptyset\ \text{ for every }a\in A .
\]
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
$\sup_{u\in U}d(u,A)\le n$ says exactly that every $u\in U$ is within $n$ of some
$a\in A$, i.e.\ $U\subseteq\bigcup_{a}\overline{B}({a, n})$; and $\sup_{a\in A}d(a,U)\le n$
says that every $a\in A$ has some $u\in U$ with $d(a,u)\le n$, i.e.\
$U\cap\overline{B}({a, n})\ne\emptyset$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:Xm}
Let $X_2=\mathbb{N}\times\{0,1\}$, and for $(n,i),(n',j)\in X_2$ put
\[
d_2\bigl((n,i),(n',j)\bigr)=
\begin{cases}
0,&(n,i)=(n',j),\\
1,&(n,i)\ne(n',j)\ \text{ and }\ n=n',\\
2,&n\ne n'.
\end{cases}
\]
We call the sets $C_n=\{n\}\times\{0,1\}$ the \emph{clusters} of $X_2$, and write
$\pi(x)=n$ when $x\in C_n$; for $A\in\mathcal{K}({X_2})$ we write
$\pi[A]=\{n\in\mathbb{N}:A\cap C_n\ne\emptyset\}$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:cluster-maps}
Let $f\colon X_2\to X_2$ be a bijection. Then $f$ is nonexpansive if and only if it
maps each cluster \emph{into} a cluster, and $f$ is an isometry if and only if it
maps each cluster \emph{onto} a cluster.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
The proof follows directly from the definition of the metric $d_2$ and the fact that $(C_n)_n$ forms a partition of $X_2$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:Xm-plastic}
The space $(X_2,d_2)$ is plastic.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Let $f:X_2\to X_2$ be a nonexpansive bijection. By Lemma~\ref{lem:cluster-maps}, $f$
maps each cluster $C_n$ into a cluster $C_{\sigma(n)}$. Since $|C_n|=|C_{\sigma(n)}|
=2$ and $f$ is injective, we conclude that $f[C_n]=C_{\sigma(n)}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:cluster-maps} again, $f$ is an isometry.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{counterexample}
The space $\mathcal{K}({X_2})$ is not plastic.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
For a finite nonempty set $F\subset\mathbb{N}$, put $K_F=\{A\in\mathcal{K}({X_2}):\pi[A]=F\}$, so that
$\mathcal{K}({X_2})$ is the disjoint union of the sets $K_F$. The definition of $d_2$ gives the following description of the Hausdorff metric:

\[
d_H\bigl(A,B\bigr)=
\begin{cases}
0,&A=B,\\
1,& A\ne B\ \text{ and }\ \pi[A]=\pi[B],\\
2,& \pi[A]\ne\pi[B].
\end{cases}
\]

Thus, $\mathcal{K}({X_2})$ has the same metric pattern as $X_2$: it is partitioned into the clusters
$K_F$, with two distinct points in the same cluster at distance $1$ and points in
distinct clusters at distance $2$. In particular, a bijection of $\mathcal{K}({X_2})$ is
nonexpansive if and only if it maps each $K_F$ into some $K_{F'}$, and it is an
isometry if and only if it maps each $K_F$ onto some $K_{F'}$. Observe that, unlike in $X_2$, where all clusters have the same cardinality, the clusters $K_F$ may have different cardinalities. This variation in cardinality allows us to construct a nonexpansive bijection that is not an isometry. 

Enumerate as $D_0,D_1,D_2,\dots$ the clusters $K_F$ with $|F|=1$, and enumerate
$E_0,E_1,\dots$ those with $|F|=2$; thus $|D_i|=3$ and $|E_j|=9$ for all $i,j$.
We define $f\colon\mathcal{K}({X_2})\to\mathcal{K}({X_2})$ as follows:

\begin{enumerate}
\item Define $f$ so that it maps $D_0\cup D_1\cup D_2$
bijectively onto $E_0$, and maps $D_i$ onto $D_{i-3}$ for every $i\geq 3$.
\item $f$ maps $E_j$ onto $E_{j+1}$ for every $j\geq0$.
\item $f$ is the identity in all remaining cases.
\end{enumerate}
The images in these three cases are pairwise disjoint and cover the whole hyperspace. Moreover, each cluster is mapped into a cluster. Thus $f$ is a nonexpansive bijection, but it is not an isometry. Indeed, if $A\in D_0$ and $B\in D_1$, then $d_H(A,B) = 2$, but $d_H(f(A), f(B)) = 1$, because $f(A), f(B)\in E_0$ are in the same cluster.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:graph}
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a connected graph. For $u,v\in V$ set
\[
d(u,v)=\min\{\,n\ :\ \text{there is a walk of length } n \text{ from } u \text{ to } v\,\}.
\]
Then $d$ is a metric on $V$, called the \emph{path metric}, and the pair $(V,d)$ is
called a \emph{graph metric space}. Note that $d(u,v)=1$ if and only if $u\sim v$, so
that the graph is recovered from the metric.  A walk of minimal length realizing
$d(u,v)$ is automatically a path, and we call it a \emph{geodesic} from $u$ to $v$.

If each edge $e\in E$ carries a weight $\ell(e)>0$ (a weighted graph), the
infimum of the sums of edge weights over walks joining two vertices defines
the \emph{weighted path distance}. Whenever distinct vertices have positive
distance, this is a metric, called the \emph{weighted path metric}, and
$(V,d)$ is then called a \emph{weighted graph metric space}. A common positive
lower bound for the edge weights is sufficient for this nondegeneracy.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:weighted}
Let $X=\{z\in\mathbb{Z}:z<0\}\cup\{2n:n\in\mathbb{N}\}$, regarded as a metric subspace of $\mathbb{Z}$, and let
$f\colon X\to X$ send each element to its predecessor in the natural ordering of
$X$. Then $f$ is a nonexpansive bijection and $d(f(0),f(2))=1<2=d(0,2)$, so $X$ is
not plastic. Note that $X$ is a weighted, 2-regular graph metric space.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{countable}
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a connected, locally finite graph. Then
every ball $\overline{B}({v, n})$ is finite, and $V$ is countable.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Fix $v\in V$. We argue by induction on $n$ that $\overline{B}({v, n})$ is finite. This is clear for
$n=0$, and $\overline{B}({v, n+1})=\bigcup_{u\in \overline{B}({v, n})}\overline{B}({u, 1})$ is a finite union of finite sets.
Since $G$ is connected, $V=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\overline{B}({v, n})$ is a countable union of finite
sets.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{isometry-automorphism}
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a connected graph and let $f\colon V\to V$ be a bijection. Then $f$
is an isometry if and only if
\[
u\sim v \iff f(u)\sim f(v)
\qquad\text{for all } u,v\in V .
\]
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
If $f$ is an isometry, then $d(f(u),f(v))=d(u,v)$; in particular, $d(f(u),f(v))=1$ if and only if $d(u,v)=1$. Conversely, suppose $f$ preserves adjacency in both directions. Then $f$ sends paths to paths, and also, $f^{-1}$ sends paths to paths, from which we conclude that $f$ is an isometry.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{Plasticity-regular-graph}
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a connected, locally finite, regular graph. Then $G$ is plastic.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Let $f\colon V\to V$ be a nonexpansive bijection and let $v\in V$. By
Lemma~\ref{general_fact_injectivity}, $f[\overline{B}({v, 1})]\subset \overline{B}({f(v), 1})$. Since $G$ is
regular, $|\overline{B}({v, 1})|=|\overline{B}({f(v), 1})|<\infty$, and injectivity of $f$ therefore implies
that $f$ maps $\overline{B}({v, 1})$ bijectively onto $\overline{B}({f(v), 1})$. In particular, $u\sim v$ if and
only if $f(u)\sim f(v)$. By Lemma~\ref{isometry-automorphism}, $f$ is an isometry,
and therefore $G$ is plastic.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:tree}
A \emph{tree} is a connected acyclic graph. For $k\ge2$ we write $T_{k}$ for the (infinite) \emph{regular tree of degree $k$}, that is, the unique tree in which every vertex has exactly $k$ neighbours.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{trees-plastic}
Let $T$ be a tree and let $f\colon T\to T$ be a nonexpansive bijection. Then $f$
carries geodesics to geodesics. Consequently $f$ is an isometry, and every tree is
plastic.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Fix $u\in T$. We prove by induction on $n$ that for every $v\inS({u, n})$ the image
under $f$ of the geodesic from $u$ to $v$ is a geodesic from $f(u)$ to $f(v)$.

For $n=0$ there is nothing to prove. For $n=1$, the claim follows because $f$ is
nonexpansive and injective, so that $d(f(u),f(v))=1$.

Assume that the statement holds for $n$, and let $v\inS({u, n+1})$, with geodesic
$$u=v_0,v_1,\dots,v_n,v_{n+1}=v.$$ Since $T$ is a tree, it contains no cycles; therefore, $v_n\inS({u, n})$ and
$u=v_0,\dots,v_n$ is the geodesic from $u$ to $v_n$.  By the induction hypothesis
$f(v_0),\dots,f(v_n)$ is a geodesic from $f(u)$ to $f(v_n)$. Since $d(v_n,v_{n+1})=1$ and $f$ is nonexpansive and
injective, $d(f(v_n),f(v_{n+1}))=1$. Moreover, $f(v_{n+1})\notin\{f(v_0),\dots,f(v_n)\}$
because $f$ is injective. Hence
\[
f(v_0),f(v_1),\dots,f(v_n),f(v_{n+1})
\]
is a simple path in $T$. In a tree every simple path is the unique path between its
endpoints, hence a geodesic, and therefore $d(f(u),f(v))=n+1=d(u,v)$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:adjacent-twins}
Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space. Two distinct points $u,v\in X$ are \emph{adjacent
twins} if $\overline{B}({u, 1})=\overline{B}({v, 1})$.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:twins-equiv}
Let $G$ be a connected graph and let $u\ne v$ be vertices. Then $\overline{B}({u, 1})=\overline{B}({v, 1})$ if and
only if $u\sim v$ and $d(u,z)=d(v,z)$ for every vertex $z\notin\{u,v\}$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Suppose $\overline{B}({u, 1})=\overline{B}({v, 1})$. Then clearly $u\sim v$. Let $z\notin\{u,v\}$ and
let $u=v_0,v_1,\dots,v_n=z$ be a geodesic. If $v_1=v$, then $u=v_0,v_2,\dots,v_n=z$ would be a path from $u$ to $z$ of length $n-1$, because $v_2\in\overline{B}({v, 1})=\overline{B}({u, 1})$, a contradiction. Therefore, every geodesic $u=v_0,v_1,\dots,v_n=z$ gives rise to the path $v,v_1,\dots,v_n=z$ from $v$ to $z$. This shows that $d(v,z)\leq d(u,z)$. By symmetry, we obtain the reverse inequality and conclude that $d(u,z) = d(v,z)$.

Conversely, if $u\sim v$ and $d(u,z)=d(v,z)$ for all $z\notin\{u,v\}$, then for
$z\notin\{u,v\}$ we get $z\in\overline{B}({u, 1})\iff z\in\overline{B}({v, 1})$, while $u,v\in\overline{B}({u, 1})\cap\overline{B}({v, 1})$
because $u\sim v$. Hence $\overline{B}({u, 1})=\overline{B}({v, 1})$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{def:dom}
Let $G$ be a connected graph and $A\subset G$. A set $D\subseteq A$
\emph{dominates} $A$ if $\overline{B}({a, 1})\cap D\ne\emptyset$ for every $a\in A$. Define
$$\gamma(A) = \min\{|D|: D \textrm{ dominates } A\}.$$
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:dom-bound}
Let $G$ be a connected, locally finite graph and let $A\in\mathcal{K}({G})$ be finite. Write
$q=|N[A]\setminus A|$. Then
\[
|\overline{B}({A, 1})|\ \ge\ 2^{\,|A|+q-\gamma(A)} .
\]
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Fix a dominating set $D\subseteq A$ with $|D|=\gamma(A)$. Suppose that $U\subset G$ satisfies
$D\subseteq U\subseteq N[A]$. Then $U$ is finite. Moreover, for every
$a\in A$, since $D$ dominates $A$, we have $\emptyset \neq D\cap\overline{B}({a, 1}) \subset U\cap\overline{B}({a, 1})$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:hyperball}, this gives $U\in\overline{B}({A, 1})$. There are exactly $2^{\,|N[A]|-|D|}=2^{\,|A|+q-\gamma(A)}$ subsets $U$ such that $D\subseteq U\subseteq N[A]$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{ore}
Any undirected graph $G = (V,E)$ without isolated vertices\footnote{A vertex is isolated if it is not adjacent to any other vertex of $G$.} has a dominating set $D$ such that its complement $V\setminus D$ is also a dominating set. In particular, if $G$ has $n$ vertices, then it has a dominating set of at most $n/2$ vertices.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
See \cite[Theorem 13.1.3]{Ore}.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:large-A}
Let $G$ be a connected, locally finite graph of minimum degree at least $k$, where $k\geq 1$. If $A\in \mathcal{K}({G})$ and $|A|>2^{\,k}$, then $|\overline{B}({A, 1})|>2^{k+1}-1$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Let $n=|A|$ and $q=|N[A]\setminus A|$, and let
$$I = \{a\in A: \overline{B}({a, 1})\cap A = \{a\}\}$$
be the set of isolated vertices of the subgraph induced by $A$. Set $t=|I|$. Since $2^{\,k}\ge2k$ for every
$k\ge 1$, we have $n=|A|\ge 2^{\,k}+1\ge2k+1$.

\emph{Case $t=0$.} In this case, the subgraph induced by $A$ has no isolated vertices. Then, by Proposition~\ref{ore}, $\gamma(A)\le n/2$ and hence $n-\gamma(A)\ge\lceil n/2\rceil\ge k+1$, where the last
inequality follows from $n\ge2k+1$. Lemma~\ref{lem:dom-bound} gives
$|\overline{B}({A, 1})|\ge2^{\,n + q-\gamma(A)} \ge2^{\,n-\gamma(A)}\ge2^{k+1}$.

\emph{Case $0<t<n$.} Then $I\neq\emptyset$ and $I\neq A$. Each $a\in I$ has at least $k$ neighbours outside $A$, so
$q \ge k$. Moreover, $n-t\ge2$. Indeed, for any $a\in A\setminus I$, the definition of $I$ gives $|\overline{B}({a, 1})\cap A|\ge2$ and $\overline{B}({a, 1})\cap A\subset A\setminus I$.

Consider now the subgraph $G'$ induced by $A\setminus I$. If $G'$ has an isolated vertex $v$, then every neighbour of $v$ lies outside $A$ or belongs to $I$. The latter is impossible by the definition of $I$. Hence every neighbour of $v$ lies outside $A$, so $v\in I$, a contradiction. This shows that $G'$ has no isolated vertex. By Proposition~\ref{ore}, $G'$ admits a dominating set $D'$ with $|D'|\le(n-t)/2$. Therefore,
$I\cup D'$ dominates $A$, so $\gamma(A)\le |I| +|D'|\le t+(n-t)/2$. Hence,
$$n-\gamma(A)\ge n -(t+(n-t)/2) \ge(n-t)/2\ge1.$$
Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:dom-bound}, we obtain
$$|\overline{B}({A, 1})|\ge2^{\,q+n-\gamma(A)}\ge2^{k+1}.$$

\emph{Case $t=n$.} In this case, every vertex of $A$ is isolated in the subgraph induced by $A$, and each $a\in A$ has at least $k$ neighbours outside $A$, so
$q \ge k$. In this case, we prove the inequality by defining some elements in the unit ball directly. 
\begin{enumerate}
\item Every set $U$ such that $A\subseteq U\subseteq N[A]$ is an element of $\overline{B}({A, 1})$ and there are $2^q$ such sets.
\item Define $B=N[A]\setminus A$. For each $a\in A$ and each $T\subseteq B$ with
$T\cap\overline{B}({a, 1})\ne\emptyset$, the set $V(a,T)=(A\setminus\{a\})\cup T$ belongs to $\overline{B}({A, 1})$. For each $a$, we have at least $2^q - 2^{q-k}$ subsets $T$ such that $T\subseteq B$ and $T\cap\overline{B}({a, 1})\ne\emptyset$. Observe that if $T\neq T'$, then $V(a,T)\neq V(a,T')$ and $V(a,T)\neq V(b,T')$ if $a\neq b$, because $b\in V(a,T)$, but $b\notin V(b,T)$. In particular, there are at least $n\bigl(2^{q}-2^{\,q-k}\bigr)$ sets of the form $V(a,T)$.
\end{enumerate}

Moreover, every set $U$ in the first family contains $A$, whereas no set $V(a,T')$ does. Hence the two families are disjoint. Therefore,
$$
|\overline{B}({A, 1})|\ \ge\ 2^{q}+n\bigl(2^{q}-2^{\,q-k}\bigr) = 2^{q}\bigl(1 + n\bigl(1-2^{\,-k}\bigr)\bigr)
\ \ge\ 2^{\,k}+n\bigl(2^{\,k}-1\bigr).
$$
Since $n\ge2k+1$, we have
$$|\overline{B}({A, 1})|\ \ge 2^{\,k}+n\bigl(2^{\,k}-1\bigr)\ge 2^{\,k}+(2k+1)\bigl(2^{\,k}-1\bigr) = (k+1)2^{k+1}-2k-1.
$$
Thus,
$$|\overline{B}({A, 1})| - (2^{k+1} - 1)\geq (k+1)2^{k+1}-2k-1 - 2^{k+1} + 1 = k2^{k+1}-2k = k(2^{k+1}-2)>0
$$
for $k\geq 1$. This shows that
$$|\overline{B}({A, 1})| >2^{k+1} - 1.$$
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:min-hyperballs}
Let $G$ be a connected, locally finite graph, with minimum degree $k\ge1$. Then
\[
\min_{A\in\mathcal{K}({G})}|\overline{B}({A, 1})|=2^{k+1}-1.
\]
Moreover,  $|\overline{B}({A, 1})|=2^{k+1}-1$ if and only if $A$ is a nonempty
subset of a twin class whose vertices have the minimum degree $k$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Observe that, for every $u\in G$, $|\overline{B}({u, 1})|\geq k+1$ with equality if and only if $u$ is a vertex with the smallest degree $k$. Let $p=|N[A]|\ge k+1$. If $p=k+1$, then each $N[a]\subseteq N[A]$
has at least $k+1$ elements, so $N[a]=N[A]$ for every $a\in A$.
Thus all vertices of $A$ belong to one twin class of degree
$k$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:hyperball} gives
$\overline{B}({A, 1})=\mathcal{K}({N[a]})$, of size $2^{k+1}-1$.

Suppose $p\ge k+2$. If $|A|>2^{k}$, use
Proposition~\ref{prop:large-A}. Otherwise a subset of $N[A]$ fails
to be in the ball only if it misses some $N[a]$. Each such event
has at most $2^{p-k-1}$ elements. Therefore
\[
|\overline{B}({A, 1})|\ge2^p-|A|2^{p-k-1}
=2^{p-k-1}(2^{k+1}-|A|)\ge2\cdot2^{k}=2^{k+1}.
\]
Conversely, if $A$ is a nonempty subset of a twin class of degree $k$,
then all $N[a]$, $a\in A$, coincide and have $k+1$ elements, so the first case
gives $|\overline{B}({A, 1})|=2^{k+1}-1$. This proves both the lower bound and its equality
characterization.
A singleton at a vertex of minimum degree attains the bound.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{def_quotient}
Let $G$ be a connected, locally finite graph. Write $Q_G=G/{\equiv}$ for the quotient of $G$ by the relation $u\equiv v$ if and only if $u=v$ or $u$ and $v$ are adjacent twins. Two \emph{distinct} classes $C,D$ are adjacent in
$Q_G$ if some vertex of $C$ is adjacent to some vertex of $D$.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{propertyQ}
Let $G$ be a connected, locally finite, $k$-regular graph and let $C,D\in Q_G$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $C\ne D$, then $d_Q(C,D)=d_G(c,d)$ for every $c\in C$ and $d\in D$.
In particular, $d_H(A,B)=d_Q(C,D)$ for nonempty $A\subseteq C$, $B\subseteq D$.
\item For $A\in\mathcal{K}({C})$, $c\in C$, and every integer $n\ge1$,
\[
\overline{B}({A, n})=\mathcal{K}({\overline{B}({c, n})}),
\]
where the ball on the left is in $\mathcal{K}({G})$ and that on the right is in $G$.
\item 
\[
\overline{B}({c, 1})=\bigcup_{D\in N_Q[C]}D,
\qquad \sum_{D\in N_Q[C]}|D|=k+1.
\]
In particular, $|\overline{B}({A, 1})|=2^{k+1}-1$ for every $A\in\mathcal{K}({C})$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
\item Fix $c\in C$ and $d\in D$. If $c = v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_n = d$ is a geodesic from $c$ to $d$, then, replacing each $v_i$ by its twin class and removing consecutive repetitions, we obtain a walk from $C$ to $D$. This walk contains a path of length at most $n$. In particular, $d_Q(C,D)\leq d_G(c,d)$. On the other hand, if $C = V_0,V_1,\ldots,V_n = D$ is a geodesic in $Q_G$, choose $v_0=c$, $v_n=d$ and $v_i\in V_i$ for $0<i<n$. We get a path of the same length from $c$ to $d$ in $G$. This shows that $d_G(c,d)\leq d_Q(C,D)$.

\item Let $B\in\mathcal{K}({G})$ and fix $c\in C$. Since every $a\in A$ belongs to $C$, Lemma~\ref{lem:twins-equiv} and $n\ge1$ give $\overline{B}({a, n})=\overline{B}({c, n})$ for every $a\in A$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:hyperball}, $d_H(A,B)\leq n$ if and only if $B\subseteq\overline{B}({c, n})$ and $B\cap\overline{B}({a, n})\ne\emptyset$ for every $a\in A$. Since $B$ is nonempty and all these balls coincide, the inclusion $B\subseteq\overline{B}({c, n})$ already implies the intersection conditions. In particular, $d_H(A,B)\leq n$ if and only if $d_G(c,b)\leq n$ for every $b\in B$. This shows that $\overline{B}({A, n})=\mathcal{K}({\overline{B}({c, n})})$.

\item The classes meeting $\overline{B}({c, 1})$ are precisely $N_Q[C]$ and are contained
in that ball. They form a partition of its $k+1$ vertices, proving (3).
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:extension}
Let $G$ be a connected, locally finite, $k$-regular graph. Consider $Q=Q_G$.
Let $q:Q\to Q$ be a bijective isometry such that $|q(C)|=|C|$ for every $C\in Q$.
Then there is a bijective isometry $g:G\to G$ such that
$$q(C) = g[C]=\{g(c): c\in C\}$$
for every $C\in Q$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
For every class $C\in Q$, since $|q(C)|=|C|$, fix a bijection
$f_{C}:C\to q(C)$. Now, for every $v\in G=\bigcup_{C\in Q}C$,
let $C_v\in Q$ be the unique class such that $v\in C_v$. Define
$g(v)=f_{C_v}(v)$.

Then, $g$ is a bijection from $G$ onto $G$. Let us prove that $g$ is an isometry. Let $v,w\in G$. Consider
$C_v,C_w\in Q$ such that $v\in C_v$ and $w\in C_w$. Then
$g(v)=f_{C_v}(v)\in q(C_v)$ and
$g(w)=f_{C_w}(w)\in q(C_w)$.

If $v = w$, then $d(g(v), g(w)) = d(f_{C_v}(v), f_{C_v}(v)) = 0 = d(v,w)$. Assume now that $v\neq w$.
If $C_v=C_w$, then $v$ and $w$ are adjacent twins and since $f_{C_v}[C_v] = q(C_v)\in Q$ is a twin class, we conclude that $d(v,w) = 1 = d(g(v), g(w))$.

On the other hand, suppose $C_v\ne C_w$. Since $q$ is an isometry,
$$d_Q(q(C_v),q(C_w))=d_Q(C_v,C_w).$$
Now, by Proposition~\ref{propertyQ}(1),
$d_Q(q(C_v),q(C_w))=d(g(v),g(w))$ and
$d_Q(C_v,C_w)=d(v,w)$, where we conclude
$$d(g(v),g(w))=d(v,w).$$
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{automorphism_g}
Let $G$ be a connected, locally finite, $k$-regular graph and put $Q=Q_G$.
Let $F:\mathcal{K}({G})\to\mathcal{K}({G})$ be a nonexpansive bijection. Then there is a bijective isometry
$q:Q\to Q$ such that
$$F^{-1}[\mathcal{K}({C})]=\mathcal{K}({q(C)})$$
and $|q(C)|=|C|$ for every twin class $C\in Q$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
\textbf{The function $q$}: Fix $C\in Q$. Since $C$ is a set of twins,
$|\overline{B}({C, 1})|$ has the smallest possible cardinality
(Theorem~\ref{thm:min-hyperballs}). By
Lemma~\ref{general_fact_injectivity}, it follows that $A=F^{-1}(C)$
also has a unit ball of minimum size. Thus, there is a unique class
$D\in Q$ such that $A\in\mathcal{K}({D})$. Define $q(C)=D$.

\textbf{$q$ is injective}: Observe that, since $A\in\mathcal{K}({q(C)})$, by
Proposition~\ref{propertyQ}(2) and Lemma~\ref{general_fact_injectivity} we conclude that
$$F[\overline{B}({A, 1})]=F[\overline{B}({q(C), 1})]=\overline{B}({C, 1}).$$
In particular, if $q(C)=q(D)$, then $\overline{B}({C, 1})=\overline{B}({D, 1})$.
By Proposition~\ref{propertyQ}(2), this means
$\mathcal{K}({\overline{B}({c, 1})})=\overline{B}({C, 1}) =\overline{B}({D, 1}) =\mathcal{K}({\overline{B}({d, 1})})$, for every $c\in C$ and $d\in D$. So $\overline{B}({c, 1})=\overline{B}({d, 1})$ and therefore $C=D$ because $c$ and $d$ would be twins for every $c\in C$ and $d\in D$.
This shows that the map is injective.

\textbf{$q$ preserves adjacency and class sizes}: Let $B\in\mathcal{K}({C})$
and $A=F^{-1}(B)$. As in the first paragraph, the minimum-ball criterion
shows that $A$ is contained in one twin class. Then, by
Lemma~\ref{general_fact_injectivity} and equality of the finite
cardinalities, $F[\overline{B}({A, 1})]=\overline{B}({B, 1})$ and therefore, by
Proposition~\ref{propertyQ}(2), since $\overline{B}({B, 1})=\overline{B}({C, 1})$ we conclude
$$F[\overline{B}({A, 1})]=\overline{B}({B, 1})=\overline{B}({C, 1})=F[\overline{B}({q(C), 1})].$$
In particular, $\overline{B}({A, 1})=\overline{B}({q(C), 1})$, which implies that the class containing
$A$ is $q(C)$. This proves that
$F^{-1}[\mathcal{K}({C})]\subseteq\mathcal{K}({q(C)})$. In particular, since $F$ is a bijection,
$$2^{|C|}-1\le2^{|q(C)|}-1$$
and therefore $|C|\leq |q(C)|$.

Let us prove that $q$ preserves adjacency. Let $C$ and $D$ be two
adjacent elements in $Q$. For any $A\in\mathcal{K}({C})$ and $B\in\mathcal{K}({D})$,
we have $A\in\overline{B}({B, 1})$. 
Since
$F[\overline{B}({q(D), 1})]=\overline{B}({D, 1})=\overline{B}({B, 1})$, we conclude that
$F^{-1}(A)\in\overline{B}({q(D), 1})$.
On the other hand, by the definition of $q$, we have $F^{-1}(A)\in\mathcal{K}({q(C)})$ and $F^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal{K}({q(D)}).$ 

Since $q(C)\ne q(D)$, Proposition~\ref{propertyQ}(1) implies that
$$d_Q(q(C), q(D)) = d_H(F^{-1}(A), F^{-1}(B)) = 1$$
where in the last statement we use the fact that $F^{-1}(A)\in\overline{B}({q(D), 1}) =\overline{B}({F^{-1}(B), 1})$. This proves that $q(C)$ and $q(D)$ are adjacent.
In particular,
$$q[N_Q[C]]\subseteq N_Q[q(C)].$$
Then, since $q$ is injective, Proposition~\ref{propertyQ}(3) gives
$$
k+1=\sum_{A\in N_Q[C]}|A|\le\sum_{A\in N_Q[C]}|q(A)|\le\sum_{A\in N_Q[q(C)]}|A|=k+1.
$$
This implies that
$$q[N_Q[C]]=N_Q[q(C)],$$
and moreover, $|q(D)|=|D|$ for every $D\in N_Q[C]$.
In particular, $|q(C)|=|C|$ for every class $C$  and therefore, the finite families $F^{-1}[\mathcal{K}({C})]$ and $\mathcal{K}({q(C)})$ have
the same cardinality, so we have
$$F^{-1}[\mathcal{K}({C})]=\mathcal{K}({q(C)}).$$

\textbf{$q$ is surjective}: Let $D\in Q$ and fix a class $C\in Q$.
Since $Q$ is connected, there is a path
$$q(C)=V_0,V_1,\ldots,V_n=D$$
that connects $q(C)$ and $D$. If $n=0$, then $q(C)=D$ and we are done.
Otherwise, since $q[N_Q[C]]=N_Q[q(C)]$ and $V_1$ is adjacent
to $q(C)$, there is a class $V_1'\in N_Q[C]$ such that
$q(V_1')=V_1$.
Again, if $n\ge2$, since
$$q[N_Q[V_1']]=N_Q[q(V_1')]=N_Q[V_1],$$
there exists $V_2'\in N_Q[V_1']$ such that $q(V_2')=V_2$.
Proceeding inductively, we obtain a class $V_n'\in Q$ such that $q(V_n')=V_n = D$, which proves that $q$ is surjective.

\textbf{$q$ is an isometry}: It remains to check that adjacency is also
preserved by the inverse. If $q(C)$ and $q(D)$ are adjacent, then
$q(D)\in N_Q[q(C)]=q[N_Q[C]]$. By injectivity, $D\in N_Q[C]$ and as the two classes are distinct, they are adjacent. Hence $q$ is a
bijection preserving adjacency in both directions, and
Lemma~\ref{isometry-automorphism} shows that $q$ is an isometry.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{every-regular-graph-plastic}
Let $G$ be a connected, locally finite, $k$-regular graph. Then $\mathcal{K}({G})$ is plastic.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Let $F:\mathcal{K}({G})\to\mathcal{K}({G})$ be a nonexpansive bijection. By
Theorem~\ref{automorphism_g}, there exists an isometry $q:Q_G\to Q_G$ such that
$$F^{-1}[\mathcal{K}({C})]=\mathcal{K}({q(C)})$$
and $|q(C)|=|C|$ for every class $C\in Q_G$.
Now, by Lemma~\ref{lem:extension}, there is an isometry $g:G\to G$ such that
$q(C)=g[C]$. Define $g^*(A)=\{g(a):a\in A\}$.
Since $F[\mathcal{K}({C})]=\mathcal{K}({q^{-1}(C)})$, we have
$$(g^*\circ F)[\mathcal{K}({C})]
=g^*[\mathcal{K}({q^{-1}(C)})]=\mathcal{K}({C}).$$

Define $H=g^*\circ F:\mathcal{K}({G})\to\mathcal{K}({G})$ which is a nonexpansive bijection, because $g^*$ is an isometry. Let $C\in Q_G$, $A\in\mathcal{K}({C})$
and let $n\ge1$ be an integer. Then $A$ and $H(A)$ belong to $\mathcal{K}({C})$
and therefore, by Proposition~\ref{propertyQ}(2),
$\overline{B}({A, n})=\overline{B}({H(A), n})=\mathcal{K}({\overline{B}({c, n})})$, for every $c\in C$. Fix any $c\in C$.
Since $H$ is a nonexpansive injection, by
Lemma~\ref{general_fact_injectivity} and the finiteness of these balls
we conclude that
$$H[\mathcal{K}({\overline{B}({c, n})})]=H[\overline{B}({A, n})]=\overline{B}({H(A), n})=\mathcal{K}({\overline{B}({c, n})}).$$
In particular, the restriction of $H$ is a nonexpansive bijection from
$\mathcal{K}({\overline{B}({c, n})})$ onto itself. Since $\mathcal{K}({\overline{B}({c, n})})$ is finite, and therefore
compact, by Theorem~\ref{tb-plastic} it is plastic. This shows that the
restriction of $H$ to $\mathcal{K}({\overline{B}({c, n})})$ is an isometry.
The result now follows from the fact that for every $A,B\in\mathcal{K}({G})$, there
exists $n$ such that $A,B\in\mathcal{K}({\overline{B}({c, n})})$. Thus $H$ is an isometry, and so
is $F$, since $g^*$ is an isometry.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:normalized-balls}
Let $G$ be a connected, locally finite, regular graph. For every nonexpansive
bijection $F$ of $\mathcal{K}({G})$, there is a bijective isometry $g_0$ of $G$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:normalized-balls}
F[\mathcal{K}({\overline{B}({v, n})})]=\mathcal{K}({g_0[\overline{B}({v, n})]})
\quad(v\in G,\ n\ge1).
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Consider $H = g^*\circ F$ as in the proof of
  Theorem~\ref{every-regular-graph-plastic}. Then
  $$H[\mathcal{K}({\overline{B}({v, n})})]=\mathcal{K}({\overline{B}({v, n})}).$$

  Since $H=g^*\circ F$, it follows that
  $$F[\mathcal{K}({\overline{B}({v, n})})]
  =(g^*)^{-1}[\mathcal{K}({\overline{B}({v, n})})]
  =\mathcal{K}({g^{-1}[\overline{B}({v, n})]}).$$
  To conclude, take $g_0=g^{-1}$.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{twins}
Let $X$ be a metric space containing twins $x\ne y$ with $d(x,y)=1$, and suppose that
$d(x,z)\ge1$ for every $z\in X\setminus\{x\}$. Then the map $F\colon\mathcal{K}({X})\to\mathcal{K}({X})$
defined by
\[
F(A)=
\begin{cases}
\{x,y\},&A=\{x\},\\
\{x\},&A=\{x,y\},\\
A,&\text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\]
is an isometry of $\mathcal{K}({X})$ which does not map the set of singletons onto itself. In
particular, $F$ is not induced by any isometry of $X$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
It is not difficult to construct the inverse of $F$. In particular, $F$ is a bijection. Since $F$ moves only $\{x\}$ and $\{x,y\}$,
it suffices to prove that 
$$d_H(B,\{x\})=d_H(B,\{x,y\})$$
for every $B\in\mathcal{K}({X})$, with $B\notin \{\{x\}, \{x,y\}\}$.

The equality is immediate when $B=\{y\}$. Thus, we may assume that there exists $b_0\in B$ with $b_0\notin\{x,y\}$.

Since $d(x,B)=\inf_{b\in B}d(b,x)\le\sup_{b\in B}d(b,x)$, we have
$$d_H(B,\{x\})=\sup_{b\in B}d(b,x).$$
On the other hand, for each $b\in B$, we have
$d(b, \{x,y\}) = 0$ if $b\in \{x,y\}$ or $d(b, \{x,y\}) = d(b,x)$ if $b \notin\{x,y\}$. 

By hypothesis, $d(b_0,x)\ge1$, hence
$\sup_{b\in B\setminus\{x,y\}}d(b,x)\ge1$, while the possible contributions of
$x$ and $y$ to $\sup_{b\in B}d(b,x)$ are $d(x,x)=0$ and $d(y,x)=1$. Therefore
\[
\sup_{b\in B}d(b,\{x,y\})=\sup_{b\in B\setminus\{x,y\}}d(b,x)=\sup_{b\in B}d(b,x).
\]

Moreover,
\[
d(x,B)\le\sup_{b\in B}d(b,x),\qquad
d(y,B)\le d(y,b_0)=d(x,b_0)\le\sup_{b\in B}d(b,x),
\]
since $x$ and $y$ are twins. Hence,
$$d_H(B,\{x,y\})=\sup_{b\in B}d(b,x)=d_H(B,\{x\}).$$
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:twins-main}
Let $G$ be an infinite connected, locally finite, regular graph. Then every
nonexpansive bijection of $\mathcal{K}({G})$ maps the set of singletons onto itself if and
only if $G$ has no adjacent twins. In this case, for every such bijection $F$
there is an isometry $f:G\to G$ such that $F(\{v\})=\{f(v)\}$ for every $v\in G$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Let $F:\mathcal{K}({G}) \to \mathcal{K}({G})$ be a nonexpansive bijection. By Theorem \ref{every-regular-graph-plastic}, we have that $F$ is in fact an isometry.
Suppose that $G$ has no adjacent twins. Then every class $C$ in $Q_G$ is a singleton.
By Theorem~\ref{automorphism_g}, $F^{-1}$ permutes the families $\mathcal{K}({C})$, which are singletons. In particular, $F$ maps
singletons onto singletons. This implies that there exists a map $f:G\to G$ such that 
$$F(\{v\}) = \{f(v)\}$$
for every $v\in G$ and it is not difficult to see that this map $f$ is an isometry.

Conversely, suppose that $G$ has adjacent twins $u\ne v$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:twins-equiv}, they are metric twins at distance $1$.
Lemma~\ref{twins} gives an isometry of $\mathcal{K}({G})$ which maps $\{u\}$ to
$\{u,v\}$ and therefore does not preserve singletons.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{main-regular-trees}
Let $T_{k}$ be a regular tree of degree $k\ge2$. Then $\mathcal{K}({T_{k}})$ is plastic.
Moreover, every nonexpansive bijection $F:\mathcal{K}({T_{k}})\to\mathcal{K}({T_{k}})$ maps the set of
singletons onto itself, and there is an isometry $f$ of $T_{k}$ with
$F(\{v\})=\{f(v)\}$ for every vertex $v$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
The plasticity of $\mathcal{K}({T_{k}})$ follows from
Theorem~\ref{every-regular-graph-plastic}. The second part follows from Corollary \ref{cor:twins-main} and from the fact that in a tree, there are no adjacent twins.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{connected-components}
For each $F \in \mathcal{K}({L})$, the set
$S_F=\{\, C \in \mathcal{K}({K \times L}) : \pi_L[C] = F \,\}$
is a compact clopen subset of $\mathcal{K}({K\times L})$, and it is a connected component of
$\mathcal{K}({K \times L})$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Let $C \in S_F$ and $D \notin S_F$. Since $C$ and $D$ differ in at least one point of
the second coordinate, (P1) gives $d_H(C,D) \geq 1$. In particular, $S_F$ is clopen in
$\mathcal{K}({K \times L})$. Moreover, $S_F$ is a closed subset of $\mathcal{K}({K\times F})$, which is
compact by \cite[Theorem 0.8]{nadler1978hyperspaces}, so $S_F$ is compact.

To see that $S_F$ is connected, write $F= \{v_1, \ldots, v_m\}$ and consider the map
$\varphi\colon {\mathcal{K}({K})}^m \to \mathcal{K}({K \times L})$ given by
$\varphi((C_i)_{i=1}^m) = \bigcup_{i=1}^m C_i\times\{v_i\}$. The map is onto $S_F$ and is continuous because
$\varphi[\prod_{i=1}^m B(C_i, r)] \subset B(\bigcup_{i=1}^m C_i\times\{v_i\}, r)$ for
every $r>0$ and every $(C_i)_{i=1}^m$. Since ${\mathcal{K}({K})}$ is connected
\cite[Theorem 1.13]{nadler1978hyperspaces}, so is ${\mathcal{K}({K})}^m$, and therefore $S_F$ is
connected. Since $S_F$ is both connected and clopen, it is a connected component.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{inequality_hausdorff}
Let $F_1, F_2 \in \mathcal{K}({L})$. Then $d_H(A,B)\geq d_H(F_1,F_2)$ for every $A \in S_{F_1}$
and $B \in S_{F_2}$.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
By symmetry, we may assume $d_H(F_1,F_2)=\sup_{v\in F_1} d(v,F_2)$. Since $F_1$ and
$F_2$ are finite, there exist $v_1\in F_1$ and $v_2\in F_2$ with
$d_H(F_1,F_2)=d(v_1,F_2)=d(v_1,v_2)$. Since $A\in S_{F_1}$, there exists $a\in K$ with
$(a,v_1) \in A$, and for any $(b,v)\in B$ we have $v\in F_2$, whence
$d((a,v_1),(b,v)) \geq d(v_1,v)\geq d(v_1, v_2)$. Therefore
\[
d_H(F_1,F_2) = d(v_1,v_2) \leq d\big((a,v_1),B\big)
\leq \sup_{(x,v)\in A} d((x,v),B) \leq d_H(A,B). \qedhere
\]
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{sierpinski}
If a compact connected metric space $K$ has a countable cover by pairwise disjoint nonempty
closed subsets, then the cover has exactly one member.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
See \cite[Theorem 6.1.27]{engelking}.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{component-map-general}
Let $f:\mathcal{K}({K\times L})\to\mathcal{K}({K\times L})$ be a nonexpansive bijection. Then there
is a nonexpansive bijection $h:\mathcal{K}({L})\to\mathcal{K}({L})$ such that
\[
f[S_F]=S_{h(F)}\qquad(F\in\mathcal{K}({L})).
\]
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Let $F \in \mathcal{K}({L})$. Since $S_F$ is connected (Lemma~\ref{connected-components}) and $f$
is continuous, $f[S_F]$ is connected. Hence, by Lemma~\ref{connected-components} there exists
$h(F)\in\mathcal{K}({L})$ with $f[S_F] \subset S_{h(F)}$.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Claim.} The map $h \colon \mathcal{K}({L}) \to \mathcal{K}({L})$ is a nonexpansive bijection.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Injectivity.} Let $S = \{ H \in \mathcal{K}({L}) : f[S_H] \subset S_{h(F)} \}$, so
that $F \in S$ and $f[\bigcup_{H \in S} S_H] \subset S_{h(F)}$. Let
$A\in S_{h(F)}$ and choose $P\in\mathcal{K}({L})$ such that $f^{-1}(A) \in S_P$. Then
$A \in f[S_P] \subset S_{h(P)}$. In particular, $h(P)=h(F)$ and $P \in S$. Then
\[
S_{h(F)} \subset f\Bigl[\bigcup_{H \in S} S_H \Bigr] = \bigcup_{H \in S} f[S_H].
\]
Each $f[S_H]$ is compact, hence closed, and these sets are pairwise disjoint because
$f$ is injective. Since $\mathcal{K}({L})$ is countable by (P1), we have that $S\subset \mathcal{K}({L})$ is countable. Then Lemma~\ref{sierpinski} gives
$|S|=1$, so $S=\{F\}$ and therefore, $h$ is injective. Moreover, $f[S_F]=S_{h(F)}$.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Surjectivity.} Given $F\in\mathcal{K}({L})$ and $A\in S_F$, choose $P\in\mathcal{K}({L})$ such that
$f^{-1}(A) \in S_P$. Then $A \in f[S_P] = S_{h(P)}$ and $A\in S_F$, so $F = h(P)$.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Nonexpansiveness.} Let $F_1,F_2\in\mathcal{K}({L})$ and fix $x\in K$. Then
$f(\{x\} \times F_i) \in S_{h(F_i)}$, so Lemma~\ref{inequality_hausdorff} gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
d_H(F_1,F_2)&=d_H(\{x\}\times F_1,\{x\}\times F_2)\\
&\ge d_H\bigl(f(\{x\}\times F_1),f(\{x\}\times F_2)\bigr)\\
&\ge d_H\bigl(h(F_1),h(F_2)\bigr),
\end{aligned}
\]
which proves the claim.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{main_product}
Let $K$ be a compact connected metric space and let $L$ satisfy \textup{(P1)}.
Suppose also that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(P2)] for every nonexpansive bijection $h$ of $\mathcal{K}({L})$, there exist a
bijective isometry $g:L\to L$ and nonempty finite sets
$L_1\subseteq L_2\subseteq\cdots$, with $\bigcup_nL_n=L$, such that
\[
h[\mathcal{K}({L_n})]=\mathcal{K}({g[L_n]})\qquad(n\ge1).
\]
\end{enumerate}
Then $\mathcal{K}({K\times L})$ is plastic.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Let $f:\mathcal{K}({K\times L})\to\mathcal{K}({K\times L})$ be a nonexpansive bijection.
By Lemma~\ref{component-map-general}, there is a nonexpansive bijection
$h:\mathcal{K}({L})\to\mathcal{K}({L})$ such that $f[S_F]=S_{h(F)}$ for every $F\in\mathcal{K}({L})$.

\textbf{Normalization}: By (P2), choose an isometry $g$ and sets $(L_n)_n$
such that $h[\mathcal{K}({L_n})]=\mathcal{K}({g[L_n]})$.
Define $J:K\times L\to K\times L$ by $J(x,v)=(x,g^{-1}(v))$.
Then $J$ is an isometry, and so is its induced map $J_*(A)=J[A]$.
Let $\widetilde f=J_*\circ f: \mathcal{K}({K\times L})\to\mathcal{K}({K\times L})$. Then 
$$\widetilde f[S_F] = (J_*\circ f)[S_F] = J_*[S_{h(F)}] = S_{g^{-1}[h(F)]}
$$
Define
$\widetilde h(F)=g^{-1}[h(F)]$ and let $(g^{-1})_*(A)=g^{-1}[A]$ be the map induced by $g^{-1}$ on $\mathcal{K}({L})$. Then $\widetilde f[S_F]=S_{\widetilde h(F)}$ and
$$\widetilde h[\mathcal{K}({L_n})]=(g^{-1})_*[h[\mathcal{K}({L_n})]] = (g^{-1})_*[\mathcal{K}({g[L_n]})] = \mathcal{K}({L_n}).$$

Let us prove that $\widetilde f$ restricts to an isometry from $\mathcal{K}({K\times L_n})$ into itself.

\textbf{Invariance}: Fix $n\ge1$. Let $A\in\mathcal{K}({K\times L_n})$ and suppose
$A\in S_F$. Then $F=\pi_L[A]\subseteq L_n$, so
$\widetilde h(F)\subseteq L_n$. Since
$\widetilde f(A)\in S_{\widetilde h(F)}$, we conclude that
$\widetilde f(A)\in\mathcal{K}({K\times L_n})$.
This shows that $\widetilde f[\mathcal{K}({K\times L_n})]\subset \mathcal{K}({K\times L_n})$.

To prove surjectivity of this restriction, let $B\in\mathcal{K}({K\times L_n})$
and write $E=\pi_L[B]\subset L_n$. Since
$\widetilde h[\mathcal{K}({L_n})]=\mathcal{K}({L_n})$, there exists $F\in\mathcal{K}({L_n})$ such that
$\widetilde h(F)=E$. Moreover,
$\widetilde f[S_F]=S_{\widetilde h(F)} = S_E$, so there is $A\in S_F$ with $\widetilde f(A)=B$.
As $F\subseteq L_n$, this set $A$ belongs to $\mathcal{K}({K\times L_n})$.
Thus $\widetilde f$ restricts to a nonexpansive bijection of
$\mathcal{K}({K\times L_n})$ onto itself.

\textbf{Isometry}: Since $L_n$ is finite and $K$ is compact, $K\times L_n$
is compact. By Proposition~\ref{hyper-total-bound},
$\mathcal{K}({K\times L_n})$ is plastic, and therefore the restriction of
$\widetilde f$ to this space is an isometry.
Now let $A,B\in\mathcal{K}({K\times L})$. Their projections onto $L$ are finite, and
the sets $L_n$ are increasing with union $L$. Hence there is $n$ such that
$\pi_L[A]\cup\pi_L[B]\subseteq L_n$. It follows that
\[
d_H(A,B)=d_H(\widetilde f(A),\widetilde f(B))
       =d_H(f(A),f(B)),
\]
where the last equality holds because $J_*$ is an isometry.
This shows that $\widetilde f$ is an isometric bijection. Since $\widetilde f=J_*\circ f$ and $J_*$ is also an isometric bijection, it follows that $f$ is an isometry and therefore, $\mathcal{K}({K\times L})$ is plastic.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:product-regular}
Let $K$ be a compact connected metric space and let $G$ be an infinite connected,
locally finite, regular graph. Then $\mathcal{K}({K\times G})$ is plastic.
In particular, $\mathcal{K}({K\times T_k})$ is plastic for every $k\ge2$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
Condition (P1) follows from Lemma~\ref{countable}. For every nonexpansive
bijection $h$ of $\mathcal{K}({G})$, Corollary~\ref{cor:normalized-balls} gives an
isometry $g$ such that
$h[\mathcal{K}({\overline{B}({v, n})})]=\mathcal{K}({\overline{B}({g(v), n})})=\mathcal{K}({g[\overline{B}({v, n})]})$ for every integer $n\ge1$. For a fixed $v$, define $L_n = \overline{B}({v, n})$ for every $n\geq 1$. This gives condition (P2), so
Theorem~\ref{main_product} applies.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{ex:nonplastic}
Let $G$ have vertex set $\mathbb{Z}$ and edges $z\sim z+1$ for every $z\in\mathbb{Z}$, together
with $n\sim n+2$ for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ (with $0\in\mathbb{N}$). Then $G$ is connected and
locally finite. Consider the shift $f(z)=z+1$. Then $f$ is a nonexpansive bijection. However, $d(-1,1)=2$
while $f(-1)=0\sim2=f(1)$, so $f$ is not an isometry and $G$ is not plastic. Observe that $G$ is a nonregular graph metric space containing cycles.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
Let $(X,d)$ be a finite metric space. Put
\[
\delta(X)=\sum_{\{a,b\}\subseteq X,\ a\ne b}d(a,b),
\]
where each unordered pair is counted once.
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{plastic-pairs}
Let $X$ and $Y$ be finite metric spaces and let $F\colon X\to Y$ be a nonexpansive
bijection with $\delta(X)\le\delta(Y)$. Then $F$ is an isometry.
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
See \cite[Theorem 2.1]{KZpairs}.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{general_finite_minimum}
Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space in which every ball is finite. Put
$m=\min\{|\overline{B}({x, 1})|:x\in X\}$ and $X'=\{x\in X:|\overline{B}({x, 1})|=m\}$. If $X'$ is finite, then
$X$ is plastic.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Let $f\colon X\to X$ be a nonexpansive bijection. If $f(x)\in X'$ then
$|\overline{B}({x, 1})|\le|\overline{B}({f(x), 1})|=m$ by Lemma~\ref{general_fact_injectivity}, so $x\in X'$ by
minimality. Then $f^{-1}[X']\subseteq X'$ and hence $X'\subseteq f[X']$. As $X'$
is finite and $f$ is injective, $f[X']=X'$, so $f$ permutes the finite set $X'$.
Choose $x\in X'$ and $N\ge0$ with $f^{N+1}(x)=x$.

Fix $r>0$. By Lemma~\ref{general_fact_injectivity},
$f[\overline{B}({f^{i}(x), r})]\subseteq\overline{B}({f^{i+1}(x), r})$ for every $i$, so
\[
|\overline{B}({x, r})|\le|\overline{B}({f(x), r})|\le\cdots\le|\overline{B}({f^{N+1}(x), r})|=|\overline{B}({x, r})|.
\]
In particular, all these cardinalities are equal. By Lemma~\ref{general_fact_injectivity}, $f$
restricts to a nonexpansive bijection of $\overline{B}({f^{i}(x), r})$ onto $\overline{B}({f^{i+1}(x), r})$, so
$\delta(\overline{B}({f^{i+1}(x), r}))\le\delta(\overline{B}({f^{i}(x), r}))$. Using again the fact that $f^{N+1}(x)=x$, we conclude that $\delta(\overline{B}({x, r}))=\delta(\overline{B}({f(x), r}))$. Thus $|\overline{B}({x, r})|=|\overline{B}({f(x), r})|$ and
$\delta(\overline{B}({x, r}))=\delta(\overline{B}({f(x), r}))$ for every $r$. By Lemma~\ref{plastic-pairs}, the restriction of $f$ to $\overline{B}({x, r})$ is an isometry onto $\overline{B}({f(x), r})$ for every $r>0$. Since any two points of $X$ belong to a common ball $\overline{B}({x, r})$, it follows that $f$ is an isometry.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:finite-min-degree}
Let $G$ be an infinite connected, locally finite graph, $k$ its minimum degree and
$G'=\{v:\deg(v)=k\}$. If $G'$ is finite, then both $G$ and $\mathcal{K}({G})$ are plastic.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
All balls of $G$ are finite by Lemma~\ref{countable}, and the set of vertices at
which $|\overline{B}({v, 1})|$ is minimal is exactly $G'$, so
Theorem~\ref{general_finite_minimum} applies to $G$.

All balls of $\mathcal{K}({G})$ are finite as well. Indeed, Lemma~\ref{countable} shows that finite-radius neighbourhoods of finite subsets of $G$ are finite, and Lemma~\ref{lem:hyperball} then gives the finiteness of the corresponding Hausdorff balls. Let $M$ be the family of sets minimizing $|\overline{B}({A, 1})|$ in $\mathcal{K}({G})$.
Since $G$ is infinite and connected, $k\ge1$, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:min-hyperballs} gives
\[
M=\bigcup_{\substack{C\in Q_G\\ C\subseteq G'}}\mathcal{K}({C})
\subseteq\mathcal{K}({G'}).
\]
As $G'$ is finite, so is $M$. Thus
Theorem~\ref{general_finite_minimum} applies to $\mathcal{K}({G})$ as well.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- question-3: body_md -->
Let $G$ be a plastic infinite connected, locally finite graph. Is $\mathcal{K}({G})$ plastic?
<!-- end question-3 -->
